stories.title: Affiliated Closes Financing on Mixed-Income Fort Lauderdale Apartment Venture
stories.excerpt: Affiliated Development has closed on a $74 million construction loan with Pacific Life Insurance Company for The Cove, a mixed-use, mixed-income multifamily development on the northwest corner of Sunrise Boulevard and Federal Highway in Fort Lauderdale. Just over half of the 374 units will be restricted to families earning 120% of the Area Median Income. In exchange for the rent restrictions, Fort Lauderdale and Broward County offered tax rebates. The Cove will rise on the site of a former hotel property. The site was home to the Clarion Inn and The Link hotel until it was recently demolished. Moss Construction is serving as general contractor on The Cove. Rinka is the project’s architect. The project is being capitalized with a $74 million construction loan from Pacific Life Insurance Company, equity from Affiliated Housing Impact Fund, LP and family office capital partners. Construction on The Cove is expected to commence immediately following closing. The post Affiliated Closes Financing on Mixed-Income Fort Lauderdale Apartment Venture appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Affiliated Development closed $74M construction loan from Pacific Life for 374-unit mixed-income Fort Lauderdale project.
50% of units restricted to 120% AMI; Fort Lauderdale and Broward County offered tax rebates for affordability.
Development on former hotel site (Clarion Inn, The Link); construction commencing immediately.
stories.summary: Affiliated Development has secured $74 million in construction financing from Pacific Life Insurance Company for The Cove, a 374-unit mixed-use, mixed-income apartment community at Sunrise Boulevard and Federal Highway in Fort Lauderdale. Over half the units are restricted to families earning 120% of AMI, with Fort Lauderdale and Broward County providing tax incentives in exchange. The project converts a recently demolished hotel site and is beginning construction immediately with Moss Construction as GC.
stories.impact: Tax incentive structures (rebates for AMI-restricted units) signal Fort Lauderdale's competitive position for affordable multifamily capital and development. This lowers effective development cost and improves equity returns for mixed-income projects, making Fort Lauderdale a more attractive market for similar deals—watch for increased affordable multifamily pipeline in South Florida.

stories.title: Olmstead Signs Luckin Coffee to 10-Year Lease in Hudson Square
stories.excerpt: Olmstead Properties has signed Luckin Coffee to a new 10-year, 1,200-square-foot retail lease at 180 Varick St., bringing one of the country’s fastest-growing coffee brands to the base of the historic Hudson Square office building. Luckin Coffee will replace a neighborhood pizzeria and deli that had occupied the storefront for more than 40 years before its longtime owner retired. Steven Marvin of Olmstead Properties represented ownership. “Luckin Coffee is an outstanding addition to 180 Varick St. and exactly the type of tenant we were seeking for the building,” said Marvin. “As Hudson Square continues to evolve as one of Manhattan’s most dynamic office neighborhoods, we’re focused on bringing in amenities that enhance the daily experience for our tenants while serving the surrounding community. Luckin has built a strong following by delivering a modern, convenient coffee experience, and we’re excited to welcome them to the building.” 180 Varick St. has been owned by the Rosenblatt family since it was developed in the 1920s by Sam Rosenblatt’s great-grandfather, making it Olmstead Properties’ longest-held asset. The post Olmstead Signs Luckin Coffee to 10-Year Lease in Hudson Square appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Luckin Coffee signed 10-year, 1,200-SF retail lease at 180 Varick St., Hudson Square, Manhattan.
Replaces 40-year neighborhood pizzeria/deli; historic office building owned by Rosenblatt family since 1920s.
Tenant mix signals evolution of Hudson Square as dynamic office neighborhood with modern amenities.
stories.summary: Olmstead Properties has leased 1,200 square feet of retail space at 180 Varick Street in Hudson Square to Luckin Coffee for 10 years. The fast-growing coffee brand replaces a long-standing neighborhood pizzeria and deli. The historic office building, owned by the Rosenblatt family since development in the 1920s, is being repositioned with modern retail anchors to enhance the tenant experience.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily impact. However, amenity-focused retail leasing in Hudson Square reflects landlord confidence in office occupancy and worker return; strong retail interest suggests underlying office market strength that may support future mixed-use or residential conversions in the submarket. Signals Hudson Square remains a destination for Class-A tenants.

stories.title: Northmarq Arranges Refi for Grocery-Anchored Queens Retail
stories.excerpt: Northmarq’s New York Metro Debt + Equity team led by Robert Delitsky and Keith Braddish arranged the $15-million refinance of Atlantic Plaza Shopping Center. The 34,949-square-foot, multi-tenant anchored center is located at 102-20 Atlantic Avenue in the Ozone Park section of Queens. Northmarq arranged the financing on behalf of the owner, Schuckman Realty Inc., through a relationship with a commercial bank. “We are thrilled to have arranged this financing for our long-time client on this premier retail center,” Delitsky said. “This transaction reflects the continued strength of well-located retail properties in the boroughs and Northmarq’s ability to deliver financing solutions to meet our clients’ objectives.” Added Ken Schuckman, president of Schuckman Realty, “Grocery-anchored retail in the boroughs is as strong as we’ve ever seen it — well-located neighborhood centers with daily-needs tenants are outperforming the market, and lenders know it.” Built in 1984, Atlantic Plaza Shopping Center is leased to daily-needs tenants including Bravo Supermarkets, Lenox Hill Radiology, Four Leaf Federal Credit Union and Dunkin’. The post Northmarq Arranges Refi for Grocery-Anchored Queens Retail appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Northmarq arranged $15M refinance of Atlantic Plaza Shopping Center (34,949 SF) in Ozone Park, Queens.
Grocery-anchored center with Bravo Supermarkets, Lenox Hill Radiology, Dunkin'; built 1984.

stories.summary: Northmarq's New York Metro team arranged a $15 million refinance of Atlantic Plaza Shopping Center, a 34,949-square-foot grocery-anchored retail property in Ozone Park, Queens. The property is leased to daily-needs tenants including Bravo Supermarkets, Lenox Hill Radiology, and Dunkin'. Owner commentary indicates strong and consistent demand for well-located neighborhood retail centers in the boroughs.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily relevance. However, strong refinancing activity and lender appetite for grocery-anchored retail in outer boroughs reflects robust neighborhood retail fundamentals and economic stability in areas like Ozone Park—a positive signal for mixed-use and residential developments competing for capital in those submarkets.

stories.title: Marcus & Millichap Closes $12.5M Sale of La Mesa Seniors Housing
stories.excerpt: Marcus & Millichap finalized the sale of 5035-49 Guava Ave., an 81-unit seniors affordable multifamily property located in La Mesa. The property sold for $12.5 million, or $154,320 per unit. “Age-restricted communities with long-term affordability protections are rarely available for acquisition in San Diego County,” said Christopher Zorbas, executive managing director investments. “This transaction reflects the continued demand for well-maintained affordable senior housing, and despite broader industry headwinds, we remain confident in the long-term fundamentals of the La Mesa and greater San Diego rental market.” said Graeme Henderson, director of investments. “New ownership is poised to keep providing low-income senior housing for years to come, given the property is the only senior deed restricted building with an agreement in perpetuity in the submarket.” Zorbas, Henderson, and Austin Huffman, investment specialists in Marcus & Millichap’s San Diego Del Mar office, marketed the property on behalf of the seller, a private owner, and procured the buyer, Positive Investments, based out of Los Angeles. The sale marks one of five transactions over 80 units in La Mesa and one of seven senior affordable transactions countywide in the past five years. bullets: Marcus & Millichap closed $12.5M sale of 81-unit senior affordable property in La Mesa, San Diego.
Sale price $154,320/unit; property built 1986 with long-term affordability restrictions.

stories.summary: Marcus & Millichap facilitated the sale of 5035-49 Guava Avenue, an 81-unit age-restricted affordable multifamily property in La Mesa, San Diego, for $12.5 million ($154,320/unit). The property sold to Los Angeles-based Positive Investments and features long-term affordability protections. The transaction underscores continued demand for well-maintained affordable senior housing despite broader industry headwinds.
stories.impact: Senior affordable multifamily remains a resilient, capital-attracted asset class in San Diego County despite macroeconomic uncertainty. Strong buyer interest and consistent transaction volume in La Mesa (5 of 80+ unit deals in 5 years) suggest affordable senior housing offers defensible cash flows and demonstrates investor confidence in demographic tailwinds (aging population), supporting development feasibility for similar products in high-growth West Coast metros.

stories.title: NAI DiLeo-Bram Markets Piscataway Industrial in Key Supply Chain Corridor
stories.excerpt: NAI DiLeo-Bram & Co. (NAIDB) is marketing 240 Circle Drive North, a 74,500-square-foot industrial building situated on approximately five acres in Piscataway, NJ. The property features a 6,000-square-foot office component and is suited for an owner-user buyer seeking to establish or expand their strategic foothold in this Central New Jersey supply chain corridor. The marketing assignment is being led by the NAIDB brokerage team of VPs Kyle Gerace and Chris Chiusolo alongside COO David A. Simon. The team has multi-decade familiarity with the property associated with Managing Director Chris Galiano’s involvement in past leasing transactions. Positioned within the Piscataway industrial hub, the property is easily accessible via two separate I-287 interchanges, which directly connect with the New Jersey Turnpike, Garden State Parkway, Routes 1, 18, 22, I-78 and I-80. “Opportunities of this size for user-buyers are exceedingly rare in today’s market, especially within land-constrained infill corridors,” said Gerace. “Based on the current market cycle, 240 Circle Drive North delivers the exact combination of heavy power, functional logistics infrastructure and strategic regional connectivity that modern operators require to insulate and scale their businesses.”  The post NAI DiLeo-Bram Markets Piscataway Industrial in Key Supply Chain Corridor appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: NAI DiLeo-Bram marketing 240 Circle Drive North, 74,500-SF industrial in Piscataway, NJ; 5 acres.
Central New Jersey supply chain corridor with dual I-287 access, direct connectivity to NJ Turnpike.

stories.summary: NAI DiLeo-Bram is marketing a 74,500-square-foot industrial property on approximately five acres at 240 Circle Drive North in Piscataway, New Jersey. The property features 6,000 square feet of office space and is positioned for owner-user buyers seeking to establish or expand operations in this Central New Jersey supply chain corridor. The site benefits from dual I-287 interchanges with direct access to the New Jersey Turnpike and major regional routes.
stories.impact: Industrial logistics hub maturation in Central New Jersey (Piscataway) is a strong positive signal for residential demand in surrounding communities. Owner-user demand and supply chain consolidation in this infill corridor will drive employment concentration and worker housing demand in adjacent residential submarkets—a window for multifamily developers to acquire and build near logistics clusters in NJ.

stories.title: Peachtree Lends $113M on Apartments’ Conversion to Margaritaville Hotel Savannah
stories.excerpt: Tidal Real Estate Partners is “waving” hello to the opportunity to convert a Savannah, Ga., multifamily building into a Margaritaville-branded hotel. The New York City development firm just sealed $113 million of bridge debt to recapitalize and repurpose the 2023-built Ann Street Lofts property into the 230-key Margaritaville Hotel Savannah, Commercial Observer has learned Peachtree Group originated the three-year floating-rate loan with two 12-month extension options for the multifamily-to-hospitality conversion project in Downtown Savannah. The conversion project is slated to commence late this summer. Jared Schlosser, head of credit originations at Peachtree Group, said after developing Ann Street Lofts as Georgia’s first large-scale mass timber multifamily project, Tidal opted to pivot the 232-unit property to hotel use after evaluating market conditions. Schlosser noted that the property is positioned for success given Savannah’s strong tourism numbers, with more than 18 million annual visitors coupled with a limited lodging supply within the city’s Historic District. “There’s a lot of development happening in this immediate area and a lot of planned development happening in this immediate area,” Schlosser told Commercial Observer. “The market continues to have a big influx of tourism and conferences so there is a good mix of demand drivers.” Walker & Dunlop negotiated the debt with a team led by Michael Brown and Keith Kurland. The Margaritaville Hotel Savannah is slated to debut in summer 2027. It will include a hotel pool deck, a Jimmy Buffett’s Margaritaville restaurant concept, and a LandShark Bar & Grill. Schlosser said the hotel will be designed for both leisure travelers as well as local residents seeking food, beverage and resort-style amenities. The conversion project is slated to commence in late summer. The pivot reflects market evaluation indicating stronger hotel demand fundamentals than multifamily, leveraging Savannah's 18+ million annual visitors.
stories.impact: Multifamily-to-hotel conversions signal a shift in Savannah's demand dynamics; rapid tourist recovery post-pandemic and strong hospitality fundamentals are outcompeting new multifamily absorption in the downtown submarket. This suggests caution for new multifamily starts in Savannah's tourism-heavy core—developers should focus on residential infill away from competing hospitality conversion zones and monitor tourism elasticity closely.

stories.title: AI Is Rewiring the Office-Leasing Playbook
stories.excerpt: Much of the conversation around artificial intelligence and commercial real estate leasing has focused on whether AI will bring people back to the office. I think that’s the wrong question. The more important one is where AI companies are choosing to invest, hire and build because those decisions tell us far more about the next office cycle than return-to-office policies. After 20 years in commercial real estate, I’ve learned to be skeptical of bold predictions. I’ve watched plenty of cycles get oversold, but this one feels different, and the data tells us why. Start with where demand is actually concentrating. One submarket in San Francisco — the non-core central business district, including South of Market and Mission Bay — is responsible for 25 percent of all active AI office demand across the markets we track. San Francisco’s South Financial District accounts for another 16 percent, San Jose another 14 percent, and New York City’s Midtown South and Midtown another 11 percent and 8 percent, respectively. Ryan Masiello. These five submarkets across three markets account for nearly three-quarters of current AI square footage. National AI office demand is up 85 percent year-over-year, but, across the industry’s largest AI hubs, demand is up 179 percent. The story isn’t simply growth — it’s concentrated growth. Today’s market is fundamentally different from the last tech cycle. OpenAI raised $122 billion in February at an $840 billion valuation. Anthropic followed with $30 billion in a Series G at $380 billion. These aren’t 2022-era companies burning headcount against speculative valuations — both are scaling revenue far faster than headcount. Not only are current fundamentals far more sound, but the market opportunity is massive. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang recently stated that writing code is not the job of a software engineer. bullets: AI office demand concentrated: 25% in SF SOMA/Mission Bay, 16% SF South Financial District, 14% San Jose.
NYC Midtown South + Midtown combined 19%; five submarkets across three metros represent ~75% of AI office demand.

stories.summary: AI companies are concentrating office demand in specific, high-tech-affinity submarkets rather than broadly returning to the office. San Francisco's South of Market and Mission Bay account for 25 percent of all tracked AI office demand, with San Francisco's South Financial District adding 16 percent and San Jose another 14 percent. NYC's Midtown South and Midtown combined represent 19 percent. These five submarkets across three metros represent nearly three-quarters of all AI office leasing activity.
stories.impact: Hyperlocal office demand concentration in AI hubs (SOMA/Mission Bay, South Financial, San Jose, Midtown South/Midtown) will drive stratified rent growth and capital competition in those specific corridors. Multifamily developers should prioritize residential sites within 0.5 miles of these AI-demand nodes and build for young, high-income tech workers—expect rents and cap rates to compress in AI submarket adjacency zones while adjacent markets lag, creating arbitrage and risk differentiation.

stories.title: Legal AI Firm Sandstone Signs 14K-SF Lease at 141 East Houston Street
stories.excerpt: An artificial intelligence-powered management platform designed to help law firms has signed an office lease on the Lower East Side, Commercial Observer has learned. AI platform Sandstone signed a five-year deal spanning 13,794 square feet on the entire third and fourth floors of East End Capital’s 141 East Houston Street, according to landlord broker Current Real Estate Advisors. Asking rent for the space was $93 per square foot. “This transaction is another example of what we’re continuing to see across the market,” Current’s Adam Henick, who represented the landlord alongside Rob Kluge, said in a statement. “We believed early on that delivering a newly built, fully furnished space with a premium level of finish would give the building a real competitive advantage, and this lease validates that strategy. When landlords invest in creating a best-in-class product, the market continues to reward it.” Newmark represented the tenant, which is relocating from 45 Main Street in Brooklyn, but the brokerage did not immediately respond to a request for comment. East End Capital developed the 63,000-square-foot property between Forsyth and Eldridge streets with Grandview Partners and Greg Kraut’s KPG Funds between 2020 and 2022 with designs by Roger Ferris + Partners. At the time, the project signaled a different kind of development pattern in the trendy enclave. Built on the site of the historic Sunshine Cinema, it’s unclear where the building stands in terms of occupancy, but it was around 50 percent full when the owners refinanced the property with a $79.6 million from Fortress in 2022. That same year, a private dining club that sold memberships through non-fungible tokens (remember those?) known as the Flyfish Club signed an 11,000-square-foot lease for three stories in the building. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Sandstone (legal AI platform) signed 5-year, 13,794-SF lease covering floors 3–4 at 141 East Houston Street.
Relocated from Brooklyn; Current Real Estate Advisors brokered landlord side; East End Capital ownership.
Newly built, fully furnished premium-finish space; landlord investment in Class-A product driving competitive leasing.
stories.summary: AI-powered legal management platform Sandstone has signed a five-year lease for 13,794 square feet (entire floors 3 and 4) at 141 East Houston Street on the Lower East Side of Manhattan. The company relocated from Brooklyn. Current Real Estate Advisors represented the landlord (East End Capital), noting that landlord investment in newly built, fully furnished, premium-finish office space is validating the competitive office market strategy.
stories.impact: AI talent migration to Lower East Side/East Houston submarket signals emerging secondary office nodes outside traditional Midtown/Midtown South; residential developers should monitor Lower East Side demand as tech talent relocates inward from Brooklyn, suggesting potential upward rent pressure in adjacent residential submarkets. However, scale of AI adoption suggests office may still compete with multifamily for mixed-use development sites in these neighborhoods.

stories.title: Grun Group Files Plans for Pair of 99-Unit Residential Buildings in the Bronx
stories.excerpt: Real estate investment and development firm Grun Group has filed plans with the New York City Department of Buildings (DOB) to bring a pair of 99-unit residential towers to the Bronx’s Woodlawn Heights neighborhood, records show. If approved, the first of the two new buildings will be at 4241 Webster Avenue and span 59,611 square feet. This development will have 99 units across eight floors. The second building will be in the same neighborhood at 4230 Peters Place, spanning 68,733 square feet and also with 99 units. The properties are currently both parking lots. The DOB plans do not provide much more information. Grun Group did not immediately respond to Commercial Observer’s request for comment. Developers have been busy in the Bronx as of late. Catholic Homes, an affiliate of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of New York, recently secured $146.9 million in construction financing to build affordable housing at 484 East 178th Street in the Bronx. Meanwhile, the city closed on $214 million in financing to bring 288 affordable senior units to 3728 Park Avenue, while housing developer Vilson Lumaj is planning two 99-unit residential properties at 761-769 East Tremont Avenue. Grun Group itself has lately been working on several projects in the city. In Kew Gardens, Queens, Grun Group filed plans in June to build a nine-story, 108-unit residential building at 116-18 Grosnevor Lane. And in January, the firm submitted an application to construct a 94-unit apartment building at 469 Troy Avenue in East Flatbush, Brooklyn. Though unconfirmed, it is probable that Grun opted to build two 99-unit residentials at its new project in Woodlawn Heights as a way to take advantage of the city’s 485-x tax abatement program. Limiting the size of a project allows developers to reap the tax benefits of 485-x without paying the high construction wages required when building 100 or more units. Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Grun Group filed DOB plans for two 99-unit residential towers in Bronx Woodlawn Heights neighborhood.
Webster Avenue building: 59,611 SF, 8 floors; Peters Place building: 68,733 SF, 99 units; both parking lots.
Concurrent Bronx activity: Catholic Homes/Archdiocese $146.9M construction financing, city $214M for 288 senior units.
stories.summary: Grun Group has filed plans with NYC Department of Buildings to develop two 99-unit residential towers in the Bronx's Woodlawn Heights neighborhood—one at 4241 Webster Avenue (59,611 SF, 8 floors) and another at 4230 Peters Place (68,733 SF). Both properties are currently parking lots. The filings come amid a broader wave of Bronx residential development, including $146.9 million in construction financing secured by Catholic Homes and $214 million in city financing for 288 senior units elsewhere in the borough.
stories.impact: Concentrated multifamily pipeline in Woodlawn Heights and broader Bronx signals developer confidence in outer-borough demand and capital availability despite macro uncertainty. City's $214M commitment to senior affordable housing and archdiocese's $146.9M construction financing indicate strong public and institutional capital supporting Bronx multifamily development. Watch for potential labor/cost inflation and land competition in Woodlawn Heights as multiple projects compete for resources and entitlements.

stories.title: Dedeaux Properties CEO Brett Dedeaux On SoCal’s Evergreen Industrial Pull
stories.excerpt: For Dedeaux Properties, California’s infamously arduous development environment can be both a hurdle and a competitive advantage. CEO Brett Dedeaux spoke with Commercial Observer about why the firm sees Tejon Ranch as such a compelling alternative to Los Angeles County and the Inland Empire, as well as how the state’s regulations can add value to entitlements, and why the company remains committed to its home turf. Photo by Frank Hammerschmidt/picture alliance via Getty Images Brett Dedeaux: A couple of years back, we bought land from Tejon Ranch and built about 230,000 square feet with excess trailer parking. That performed well, and we sold it to an owner-user in 2024, and that led to a broader joint venture with Tejon Ranch to build out more industrial space. Labor is a big part of the appeal for any logistics company. There is affordable labor and more affordable housing in Tejon Ranch. We kind of say, “Tejon Ranch is the Texas of California.” It is a very business-friendly environment where things get done relatively quickly. It is not as overly regulated. For big-box deals, if you have to go farther and farther east to Beaumont, Banning or the High Desert, Tejon Ranch is a competitive alternative from a drayage and transportation cost standpoint. You can easily get back into the L.A. Basin, but you can also service Northern California and the Western and Northwestern U.S. We also have plentiful power at Tejon Ranch, which is really key. Then look at the San Fernando Valley. If it seceded from the City of Los Angeles, I believe it would be one of the largest cities in the country. bullets: Dedeaux Properties pivoting from LA/Inland Empire to Tejon Ranch (North of LA County) for industrial development.
Labor cost and affordable housing availability key appeal; company sold ~230K SF at Tejon in 2024 to owner-user.
Regulatory and entitlement complexity in CA creates competitive advantage for developers with deep local expertise.
stories.summary: Dedeaux Properties CEO Brett Dedeaux discusses the firm's strategic shift toward Tejon Ranch as an alternative to Los Angeles County and Inland Empire industrial development. The company purchased land at Tejon Ranch and built approximately 230,000 square feet of logistics space with excess trailer parking, which sold to an owner-user in 2024. Labor cost and affordable housing availability are primary drivers; the firm is now pursuing a broader joint venture with Tejon Ranch to expand industrial space. CEO notes that California's regulatory complexity can be a competitive moat for developers with entitlement expertise.
stories.impact: Dedeaux's northward migration to Tejon Ranch reflects rising labor/housing costs in traditional LA industrial corridors (LA County, Inland Empire), signaling cost pressure on logistics supply chains—multifamily developers should capitalize on labor-housing demand in Tejon Ranch and surrounding communities (Bakersfield area). Dedeaux's JV signals a flight from saturated industrial markets; watch for secondary/tertiary market industrial growth to drive ancillary multifamily demand. California's regulatory complexity creates a moat favoring larger, entrenched developers—consolidation may follow.
